analysis.one_liner: Lets the President suspend banking laws and rules it deems burdensome.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote and died in the Senate Banking Committee when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the President to review every federal law and regulation affecting banks and other insured depository institutions, then allowed him to suspend any of them by executive order if he judged them unnecessary, too costly, or harmful to credit availability [S2] [S3]. The bill's own findings cite an industry-estimated regulatory burden on banks of up to $17 billion and argue that relief would free up credit for small businesses [S3]. It included limits: the President could not suspend rules needed for bank safety and soundness, anti-discrimination rules, or anything tied to monetary policy, and the power would have expired on January 1, 1997 [S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never went anywhere [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and bank holding companies, which would gain a White House-controlled mechanism to shed compliance costs; the bill argues this would also ease credit for small businesses [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The President would be required to review all laws and regulations affecting insured depository institutions within 30 days of enactment and could suspend any of them by executive order upon finding they are no longer useful, cost more than they achieve, or reduce credit availability [S3].
The bill's findings cite an estimated regulatory burden on financial institutions of as much as $17 billion, which the bill says is draining capital and restricting credit to small businesses [S3].
Before suspending a rule, the President would have to consult banking regulators and notify the congressional banking committees, and the suspension power would terminate on January 1, 1997 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Depositors and consumers, who rely on banking rules for disclosure and fair treatment; any rule not explicitly exempted could be suspended for 30 days after publication, with the President able to shorten that window "for good cause" [S3]. Congress would also cede authority over its own statutes to the executive branch [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would let a single official suspend federal statutes passed by Congress, not just agency rules, subject only to consultation and notification of committees rather than congressional approval [S3].

Exemptions in the bill are narrow: they protect safety-and-soundness rules, anti-discrimination rules, monetary policy, and enforcement actions, but leave consumer-facing laws such as lending-disclosure requirements eligible for suspension [S3].

The promised credit benefit rests on the bill's own findings, including the $17 billion burden estimate attributed to a financial-industry examination council, which would not have been independently verified before suspensions began [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — easing credit for small businesses by cutting bank compliance costs — is plausible on its face, but the bill's design is an unusually blunt instrument: it would hand the President unilateral power to set aside laws written by Congress, with a short or even shortened notice period and no vote needed from either chamber [S3]. The protections in Section 7 limit the damage, but many consumer and disclosure protections would still be suspendable, and the claimed $17 billion burden was not independently verified [S3]. A more conventional route — Congress reviewing and amending specific banking rules itself — was never attempted, because the bill went nowhere in committee [S5].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Alfonse D'Amato introduced the bill on March 16, 1993, joined on introduction by Senators Shelby, Dole, Mack, Thurmond, and Domenici, and it drew eight cosponsors in total (seven Republicans and one Democrat) [S3] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs on March 16, 1993 [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history for the remainder of the 103rd Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, existing banking laws and consumer protections stayed in place, and banks gained nothing from it. Deposit-account and lending rules that could otherwise have been suspended by executive order remain in force.

for.name: Sen. Alfonse D'Amato
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed it as relief from an estimated $17 billion regulatory burden on banks to unlock small-business credit.

for.name: Senate cosponsors of S. 591 (7 Republicans, 1 Democrat)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the original cosponsors named at introduction were Senators Shelby, Dole, Mack, Thurmond, and Domenici.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee (Chair Donald Riegle)
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in its action history before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (seven Republican and one Democratic cosponsor), but it never reached a vote, so no recorded split exists.

industries.note: The bill would have let the President suspend banking laws and rules, cutting compliance costs the bill pegs as high as $17 billion [S3]. Banks' gain would come from shedding rules; depositors and borrowers would bear the risk if consumer-disclosure rules were among those suspended, though safety-and-soundness and anti-discrimination rules were exempted [S3].
The bill argues that cutting banks' regulatory costs would free capital and expand credit to creditworthy small businesses; this benefit was never tested or verified [S3].

industries.industry: Federal banking regulators (Fed, FDIC, OCC, OTS)
industries.note: Their rules and guidelines would become suspendable by executive order, weakening the rulebook they use to supervise banks, which is also the rulebook that protects depositors and borrowers [S3].
